text:
The integration of artificial intelligence into education requires teachers to develop new professional skills. Although many schools are adopting AI-supported platforms, successful implementation depends on whether educators understand how these systems work, where they are useful, and what risks they create. Teacher training is therefore essential to ensure that AI improves learning rather than adding confusion or weakening professional judgement.

Teachers first need practical knowledge of how to use AI tools in lesson planning, assessment, and student support. AI may help generate practice questions, suggest activities, summarise materials, or provide preliminary feedback. However, educators must evaluate these outputs carefully because they may contain inaccuracies, bias, or unsuitable content.

Training should also address academic integrity. Teachers need clear methods for distinguishing acceptable assistance from work that has been substantially produced by AI. Rather than relying only on detection software, educators should learn how to redesign assignments, examine drafts, conduct oral follow-ups, and assess the learning process.

Another important area is data privacy. Teachers may unintentionally expose student information by uploading assignments, personal details, or performance records to external AI platforms. Professional development should therefore explain data protection rules, approved tools, and safe handling practices.

AI literacy must also include ethical and pedagogical judgement. Teachers should understand that efficiency is not the only goal of education. A tool that produces faster answers may still reduce discussion, creativity, or independent thought. Educators need confidence to reject AI use when it does not serve a clear learning purpose.

Teacher training is central to responsible AI adoption in education. Educators require technical knowledge, ethical awareness, and practical strategies for assessment and classroom use. AI can support teachers effectively only when they remain capable of questioning its outputs and deciding when human instruction is more appropriate.
